strengths: The clinical motivation and design are sound: structuring generation around six anatomical regions (lung, airway, mediastinum, heart/vessels, osseous, upper abdomen) mirrors the radiologist's workflow and is a reasonable way to obtain more localized, complete reports than global-volume modeling.

The token-efficiency argument is well made: R² token pooling reduces the visual token count from D×T to D+T while retaining slice-level global tokens and region-representative tokens. The comparison against LITA-style uniform slow-token sampling (Ablation-LITA) is a relevant and useful control.

Extracting deterministic, quantitative patient-specific attributes (organ volumes, lesion count/diameter/location) from pseudo-masks and converting them into textual prompts is a practical, interpretable way to inject clinical measurements into the LLM, and the algorithm is given concretely in the supplement.

The paper is clearly written and well illustrated, and the implementation details (RAD-DINO encoder, frozen vision tower, LLaMA3-8B + LoRA, optimizer, schedules, batch sizes, ZeRO stage 2) plus a code release support reproducibility reasonably well.

The evaluation combines complementary NLG metrics with clinical-oriented LM metrics (RadBERT-based CA-F1, GREEN error analysis, LLM-as-judge), and the gains in CA-F1 and GPT-4 score are consistent across the reported configurations and the qualitative example.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The framework is largely an assembly of existing components: the mask-aware visual extractor and fixed token placement follow MAIRA-SEG [28], the fast/slow token idea follows LITA [38], masks come from SAT [53], and the data and region-grounding come from RadGenome-Chest CT [12]. The paper itself states it uses "the same hyperparameter settings as MAIRA-SEG," and R² token pooling is a modest region-centric variant of LITA-style pooling. The incremental 3D extension is not accompanied by a comparable analysis of why the existing 2D design fails in 3D.

The central SOTA claim is weakly supported by the numbers. BLEU-4 differences are within noise (M3D 0.288 vs Ours 0.290) and M3D is better on ROUGE-L (0.391 vs 0.375) and METEOR (0.497 vs 0.494); the Green score is clearly worse than CT2Rep (0.231 vs 0.374) and is dismissed post hoc as "overfitting to normal cases" without any supporting analysis. There are no error bars, no multi-seed variance, and no statistical significance testing for any comparison.

Evaluation scope and baseline fairness. All experiments use a single dataset (RadGenome-Chest CT, 1,304 test patients) with no external/cross-dataset validation. Baselines were re-trained by the authors under a self-imposed 48-hour/2×A100 budget, and the paper explicitly acknowledges CT2Rep was "insufficiently trained with limited resources" — yet CT2Rep is still used as evidence in the comparison. This confounds the headline claim, and the reported results are more accurately comparisons against re-implementations than against published numbers.

Possible annotation circularity is not examined. RadGenome-Chest CT's region-grounded reports were constructed using SAT masks, and MedRegion-CT also uses SAT pseudo-masks to build region tokens and attribute prompts. Baselines do not have equivalent access to this supervision-like signal. The paper never quantifies how much of the gain stems from aligning with the annotation pipeline that produced the ground truth rather than from the proposed visual modeling.

No clinical/human evaluation. The only 'clinical correctness' judge is GPT-4o Mini with an M3D-derived prompt, which is a noisy proxy; CA-F1 relies on RadBERT embeddings that were not validated for this generation setting. A small radiologist rating study (even on a subset) would substantially strengthen the clinical claims, especially since the paper emphasizes 'clinical relevance' and 'interpretability,' neither of which is measured.

Internal inconsistencies and reporting errors. Table 1 labels the full model as 'Ours (Ablation-R²+Attr+Mask)', which is confusing and suggests a labeling mistake; the caption references MS-VLM, which does not appear in the table or experiments; and in the ablation, Ablation-R²+Attr actually achieves a higher BLEU-4 (0.293) than the full model (0.290), which the text argues away as a 'synergy' effect rather than explaining.

Missing analyses that the claims invite: no limitations section, no societal-impact or deployment-risk discussion, no hallucination/failure analysis beyond one qualitative example, and no ablation on the number of sampled region slices s or on the quality/sensitivity of the SAT pseudo-masks (which the whole pipeline depends on).

strengths: Addresses a clinically important and challenging problem: region-focused 3D CT report generation with multimodal LLMs.
Combines several sensible components—region-representative token pooling, mask-driven visual extraction, and patient-specific attribute prompting—into a single framework.
Uses a public dataset (RadGenome-Chest CT) and provides supplementary training details, ablation studies, and a qualitative example, supporting some reproducibility.
The motivation from radiological workflow (overview, regional analysis, clinical integration) is clear and the figures communicate the overall pipeline well.
Ablation results suggest that the proposed components can improve some metrics (e.g., CA-F1 and GPT-4 score) over the tested variants.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: R^2 token pooling is largely an adaptation of fast/slow token strategies such as LITA with mask-based slice selection; the mask-driven extractor is a 3D extension of MAIRA-SEG; the patient attribution extractor is a rule-based feature-to-text pipeline. The combination is incremental rather than conceptually new.

The evaluation is not sufficient for the clinical claims. Only one dataset is used, there is no radiologist or human reader study, no per-region evaluation despite the region-focused contribution, no hallucination/faithfulness analysis, and no statistical significance or error bars on the reported differences.

Baseline comparisons are potentially unfair: the paper retrains baselines under a fixed 48-hour/2-A100 constraint and replaces or standardizes their LLM with LLaMA3-8B, which may disadvantage methods originally designed with different pretraining, architectures, or training budgets. Official baseline numbers are not used.

The state-of-the-art claim is not fully supported: the model is not best on ROUGE-L, METEOR, or Green Score, and the improvements over M3D on BLEU-4 and CA-F1 are modest. The dismissal of CT2Rep's higher Green Score as 'biased' is not supported by evidence.

The ablation table is confusing and internally inconsistent. The row labeled 'Ours (Ablation-R^2+Attr+Mask)' makes it unclear which configuration is the full model, which weakens the reader's ability to attribute gains to individual components.

Important implementation details are missing or unclear: prompt templates for the LLM, region-report merging procedure, exact pseudo-mask generation and integration during training/testing, selection of hyperparameters such as s/T, and the public code link in the main paper. This limits reproducibility.

Potential evaluation circularity: the RadGenome-Chest CT masks are generated using SAT, and the proposed method also uses SAT to generate pseudo-masks. It is unclear whether this shared segmentation source inflates performance or makes the method dependent on the same tool used to define ground truth.

The GPT-4-based evaluator lacks prompt/version/temperature details and human correlation, making one of the key clinical evaluation metrics difficult to reproduce and interpret. The paper also omits failure-case analysis and limitations discussion.

strengths: The paper proposes a region-focused 3D CT report generation framework that mirrors radiologists' workflow, combining global and region-specific information in a structured, interpretable manner.

The R² token pooling mechanism is technically sound and efficient: it reduces the visual token count from D×T to D+T while preserving both slice-level global context and region-specific details, as supported by the ablation study.

The integration of a mask-driven visual extractor and patient-specific attributes (organ volumes, lesion counts/diameters/locations) is a sensible way to inject clinical priors into an MLLM, improving clinical accuracy and interpretability.

The method is evaluated on the public RadGenome-Chest CT benchmark with several baselines and ablations, and it achieves encouraging results on CA-F1 and GPT-4-based metrics, with a qualitative example showing fewer hallucinations than competing approaches.

The supplementary material provides useful implementation details (two-stage training, LoRA, optimizer, hardware), and the abstract claims public code availability, which supports reproducibility if the link is provided in the final version.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to a single dataset (RadGenome-Chest CT) with no external or multi-institutional validation, and no human reader study; clinical validity therefore remains only partially established.

The method does not uniformly outperform baselines: M3D reports higher ROUGE-L and METEOR, and CT2Rep reports higher GREEN score. The full model's gains on CA-F1/GPT-4 are modest and lack significance tests, confidence intervals, or repeated runs.

Baseline comparison fairness is questionable: all methods are reimplemented with LLaMA3-8B under a 48-hour/2×A100 constraint, which may not reflect the original methods' optimal settings; CT2Rep in particular is designed without an LLM and may be disadvantaged by this protocol.

The ablation and main-result table are confusingly presented: the full model appears as 'Ours (Ablation-R²+Attr+Mask)' in Table 1, and the component contributions are not cleanly separated, e.g., R²+Attr improves BLEU-4 but lowers CA-F1 relative to the full model.
The pipeline depends on SAT-generated pseudo-masks, so segmentation errors can propagate into both visual tokens and textual attributes; the robustness of this dependence is not analyzed.

The evaluation may be biased toward the proposed structured output: ground-truth reports are preprocessed by splitting them into six predefined regions, and the method generates region-wise reports that are then merged, which could favor the proposed template over more general report generation.

There is no limitations section or failure-case analysis, and no discussion of dataset biases, false negatives, hallucination rates, or clinical deployment risks. Minor presentation issues also remain (e.g., 'extention', inconsistent baseline count, unclear token-count notation, no code link in the PDF).
